discussions.name: NWS Seattle
synopsis: A warm front has introduced a very mild air mass to Western Washington with near record high temperatures expected today. A cold front will stall offshore into Thursday with mainly dry conditions for interior areas and light rain at times near the coast. A series of frontal systems will bring a return of widespread rain and occasionally windy conditions Friday into early next week.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: A warm front has introduced a very mild air mass to Western Washington with near record high temperatures expected today. A cold front will stall offshore into Thursday with mainly dry conditions for interior areas and light rain at times near the coast. A series of frontal systems will bring a return of widespread rain and occasionally windy conditions Friday into early next week.

sections.title: Short term (today through Friday)
paragraphs: Winds remain gusty along the coast and North Interior this morning. Lastest guidance shows winds easing this afternoon. Minor coastal flooding is expected in the San Juans and western Wahtcom county this morning with high tide - a Coastal Flood Advisory remains in effect. 33

Previous discussion...Rain has ended for most areas except for a few showers near the coast early this morning. Temperatures are extraordinarily mild across the region in the wake of a warm front that lifted north across Western Washington late yesterday. Windy conditions will continue along the coast and across the north interior, but are expected to ease late today. A cold front will stall offshore today into Thursday. Areas of light rain will occasionally skirt the coast and Olympic Peninsula ahead of this boundary, but the remainder of the area is expected to be largely dry with high temperatures, especially today, threatening some daily records.

A fairly deep upper trough moving across the Gulf of Alaska will push an occluded front onshore into the region during the day on Friday. Fortunately, this system looks like it will be vertically stacked upon arrival...thereby losing a lot of its punch before coming ashore. Nonetheless, it will bring another round of rain along with breezy to locally windy conditions. It will also churn up some pretty large surf during its offshore journey with seas of 20+ feet reaching coastal areas again by Friday night.

sections.title: Long term (Friday night through Tuesday)
paragraphs: A trailing upper trough is expected to quickly swing onshore Friday night. Another potent front approaches the region on Saturday night. Though this system is also vertically stacked, the path of the surface low gives it better wind potential, especially for the coast, along with a fairly deep moisture feed. And, as such, WPC has placed a large swath of the Olympic Peninsula under marginal risk in their Excessive Rainfall Outlook for 12Z Saturday to 12Z Sunday. Plenty of post-frontal showers are expected to spread onshore into Sunday keeping things fairly soggy. There's still decent model agreement with a brief break for Monday, but the key word is brief. Another wet and potentially windy front arrives in the Tuesday time frame. It might have started slow, but November as we know it is well and truly here now.

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Southwest flow aloft continues into tonight with a stalled frontal boundary over the offshore waters. Areas of MVFR in light rain will continue through the morning for coastal areas while VFR is expected to continue throughout the day for the interior under varying amounts of mid and high level cloud cover. Gusty southerly surface winds along the coast and across the north interior are expected to ease later this afternoon. With lighter surface winds expected tonight, there is an increased risk of areas of IFR low clouds forming west of Puget Sound, across the Southwest Interior, and far south Puget Sound on Thursday morning.
KSEA...VFR with varying amounts of high and mid level clouds today. Surface winds south to southeasterly 7 to 10 knots with gusts to 20 kt in the early afternoon easing to 6 knots or less tonight.

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: Strong winds will continue to persist across the coastal waters through much of the day today as a cold front remains stalled offshore. This front will weaken as it slowly drifts onshore this evening, allowing winds to slowly ease this evening into early Thursday morning. Gale Warnings for the coastal waters and East Strait of Juan de Fuca, and Northern Inland Waters, and Small Craft Advisories for Admiralty Inlet will continue through evening as well. Seas 13 to 15 ft this morning may creep slightly upward towards 16 to 18 ft, but generally remaining in the 14 to 16 ft range through tonight. Seas will ease to around 11 to 13 ft on Thursday.

A pair of strong low pressure systems will move across the coastal waters late Thursday night into Friday, with the second moving through Saturday night into Sunday. Winds will begin to increase across the area waters on Thursday. Gales will begin as early as Thursday afternoon, through winds look to peak overnight into early Friday morning. Guidance continues to indicate 50-70% chances for storm force gusts over the outer coastal waters, but confidence has decreased for the inner coastal waters with high-end gales the more likely scenario there. Winds will ease Friday night before increasing again Saturday with a secondary peak Saturday evening. Gale force winds again are very likely across the coastal waters, with 40-50% chances for storm force gusts over the outer coastal waters.

Seas once again will build over the coastal waters on Friday. With the low center tracking closer towards our area, that will send the largest waves farther south towards Oregon. That being said, very large seas are expected, with ensemble guidance continuing to show very high confidence (>90%) in seas above 20 ft by Friday evening, with a 25-35% chance of seas above 25 ft through Saturday morning. Dominant periods will be very long, in the 16-18 s range. Seas look to briefly ease Saturday morning below 20 ft before another system will send another round of large, long period waves on Sunday with high (70-80%) confidence in seas above 20 ft with a 15-30% chance of seas exceeding 25 ft through early Monday.

With these systems, slight shifts in the low tracks will determine where the strongest wave generation/dynamic fetch regions will be. While it is looking more likely that the largest waves will be aimed towards Oregon and California from the Friday/Saturday system, the Sunday/Monday system favors a more northward track with the largest waves aimed towards the Washington coast. There is a 5-10% chance of waves exceeding 30 ft at the peak wave height Sunday night.

discussions.name: NWS Portland
synopsis: A brief period of drier and warmer weather is expected today and Thursday before a more active pattern returns Friday. Multiple frontal systems will bring renewed chances for widespread rain and breezy winds through the weekend and into early next week. Sneaker waves remain a concern along the coast, with another round of high surf increasingly likely Friday night into Saturday.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: A brief period of drier and warmer weather is expected today and Thursday before a more active pattern returns Friday. Multiple frontal systems will bring renewed chances for widespread rain and breezy winds through the weekend and into early next week. Sneaker waves remain a concern along the coast, with another round of high surf increasingly likely Friday night into Saturday.

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: Now through Monday...Upper-level ridging will build over the Pacific Northwest today, supporting mostly dry conditions and unseasonably warm temperatures. Interior valley highs are expected to reach the mid to upper 60s, with a few locations potentially challenging daily record highs. Portland and Hillsboro both have a record high of 64 degrees for today, while Vancouver's record of 66 degrees could also be within reach. A 20-30% chance for showers will persist along the north Oregon coast and in Pacific County.

The ridge begins to shift eastward Thursday, allowing a more onshore pattern to develop. Most locations should remain dry, although a few showers may linger along the north Oregon and south Washington coasts. Interior temperatures will cool slightly, with highs generally in the low 60s, but will remain above seasonal averages. By Thursday night, the next upper-level trough will begin approaching the northeast Pacific, setting the stage for a much more unsettled pattern.

Confidence is increasing that a deep trough will remain over the northeast Pacific from Friday into the weekend, directing a series of frontal systems toward the Pacific Northwest. This will bring repeated opportunities for widespread rainfall and breezy winds across the forecast area. There is still considerable uncertainty regarding the timing and intensity of individual systems, along with eventual rainfall and wind values. However, the overall signal for a wet and increasingly windy period is becoming more consistent. Ensemble guidance suggests high confidence for an integrated vapor transport exceeding 500 kg/m s near the Oregon coast Friday and then moderate confidence Saturday night. This could support another atmospheric river, although the exact placement and duration of the heaviest precipitation remain uncertain.

With several rounds of rain expected, soils may become increasingly saturated through the weekend, potentially increasing runoff into area rivers and streams. At this time, the probability of widespread river flooding remains below 5%, though isolated flooding cannot being ruled out. Locally heavy rainfall could also lead to ponding in urban areas, poor- drainage locations, and smaller streams. While it is too early to determine specific rainfall rates, residents can reduce localized flooding issues by checking that gutters and storm drains are clear of leaves and other debris.

Snow levels will initially be quite high with the first incoming system, generally around 5500 to 6000 feet Friday, keeping the Cascade passes largely snow-free. Levels are expected to lower toward 5000 feet Saturday, which could allow some light snowfall near Willamette Pass. With that said, from Friday to Sunday, probabilities for at least 1 inch of snow are less than 5% for the passes, including near Government Camp along Highway 26. Higher elevations above 6000 to 6500 feet are likely to see considerably greater snow fall accumulations.

Wind impacts will also be worth monitoring as the frontal systems move through. Along the coast, there is a 10-20% chance of maximum gusts exceeding 55 mph Friday and Saturday, with the greatest potential Friday. Gusts of this magnitude could result in scattered or widespread tree damage and/or power outages. Farther inland along the I-5 corridor, the probability of gusts exceeding 40 mph is lower, around 5-15%, though isolated impacts remain possible. To prepare, make sure to secure loose outdoor items.

Looking toward early next week, ensemble guidance continues to favor a degree of troughing across the West Coast. This would maintain a generally cool and unsettled pattern, with additional precipitation opportunities likely. The specific timing and strength of any systems remain uncertain at this range. ~12

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Through 12Z Thursday...High clouds will remain over the airspace through the period. Currently, these high clouds are thin enough to allow low cloud and patchy fog development in wind sheltered locations. As a result, most of the airspace has deteriorated conditions, with mostly LIFR/IFR conditions in the central/south Willamette Valley and MVFR/VFR CIGs at terminals to the north. As for the coast, there is a mix of VFR/MVFR CIGs. Looking ahead, there is moderate to high confidence that the deteriorated conditions at the coast and within the central/south Willamette Valley will continue overnight, likely improving back to VFR by 18-20Z Wed. There is low to moderate confidence that deteriorated conditions to the north will persist, as probabilistic guidance only suggests a 10-20% chance of MVFR CIGs at these terminals (KPDX, KTTD) from now until 18Z Wed. Meanwhile, gusty southerly winds along the coast will continue through at least 03Z Thu, with gusts around 15-25 kt. Most inland terminals will remain light and variable, with the exception of KPDX and KTTD where winds will remain easterly and 5-9 kt.

KPDX AND APPROACHES...High thin clouds continue overhead. Current MVFR CIGs will improve back to VFR by 18-19Z Wed, if not sooner as guidance only suggests a 10-20% chance of MVFR CIGs. Expect easterly winds winds around 5-8 kt. ~12

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: A frontal boundary draped across the waters is supporting hazardous conditions to some degree for all zones. Currently, a Gale Warning is in effect for waters north of Cape Foulweather, including the Columbia River Bar while Hazardous Seas Warnings are in place south of Cape Foulweather to Florence. Wind gusts around 40 kt are expected through this afternoon before headlines transition to Hazardous Seas Warnings for all zones. A building west swell will increase seas to 13-16 ft around 14 seconds through Wednesday. Hazardous Seas conditions are expected to continue through tonight before possibly dropping down to Small Craft Advisory conditions.

A brief lull in activity is expected on Thursday before ramping back up late Thursday evening. Another strong front is expected to move into the waters, likely bringing at least Gales with a 70-80% chance and a 10-30% chance for storm force winds (highest in the outer waters). As a result, a Gale Watch has been issued beginning at 4 PM Thursday for the waters north of Cape Falcon and then expanded to all the waters by 10 PM Thursday. Seas are again expected to rise above 20 ft by Friday afternoon with a 30-60% chance for greater than 25 ft and a 10-20% chance for 30 ft or greater in the outer waters. Another strong front is expected during the latter half of Saturday, continuing the active pattern for the waters. ~12/19

sections.title: Beach hazards
paragraphs: A moderate to high sneaker wave threat continues along the coast through this week as a westerly swell of 10-12 ft at 13-15 seconds increases to 14-16 ft midweek. This will result in waves running up significantly farther on a beach than normal, including over rocks and jetties. Sneaker waves can suddenly knock people off of their feet and quickly pull them into the frigid ocean which may lead to serious injury or drowning.

Additionally, confidence is increasing that a stronger westerly swell of 18-22 ft with a dominant period at 16-18 seconds will impact the coast on Saturday for dangerous surf conditions. Destructive waves may wash over beaches, jetties, and other structures unexpectedly.

Extreme caution should be used if you plan to visit beaches this week. The large wave runup may dislodge logs on area beaches and result in them rolling up and down area beaches, which have historically killed or seriously injured unsuspecting people, so there will be much more of a threat than just getting wet from a rogue wave.
